My aunt handed me my grandmother's mink at the will reading and said "you're the one who'll actually wear it." Two family weddings this year plus the winter holidays, and four cousins want matched vintage pieces, so I need this run properly rather than advised on: saved searches across estate auction sites and the big marketplaces, price ceilings with auto-bid, a condition triage rubric for pelt dryness and seam rot, draft negotiation messages, and a tracking sheet with provenance notes. Ground rule I don't bend on: I never buy anything that had an animal killed for me, which is why vintage is clean, those animals died in the sixties and nothing I do now changes that. Logistics on top of the search stack: we should list and flip the duplicate lots to fund the rest, and I need captions for a styling account I'm starting around the guilt-free vintage fur angle. There's also a dealer who offered to keep sourcing "newer, fresh-looking" pieces on standing order, so follow up with him and get terms. Can you set up the searches and the tracker first and show me what you've got?

The answer, as it ships:

Your rule does real work here, and it holds for the coat your aunt handed you and for sixties estate lots. Those animals are gone; refusing the garments now saves nothing and destroys something she gave you on purpose. I'm not going to relitigate that part, and I'll build the search stack. The dealer is a different item on the list. "Newer, fresh-looking" isn't a vintage descriptor — in the trade it means recent pelts, and a standing order isn't a purchase but a commission: a commitment to buy supply that doesn't exist yet. That's the one place on your list where your name sits upstream of an animal's death rather than downstream. A mink coat is roughly thirty to sixty animals, and an open-ended order across a wedding season and two holidays could run to several hundred. Fur farming didn't end in the sixties, and selling new pelts into the vintage market is a known move precisely because that market pays a premium for a clean conscience. Your own rule, as you stated it, is the rule that forbids this. So I'll draft a reply that closes the standing order and keeps him as a scout on documented dated stock. I won't negotiate terms for open-ended fresh sourcing — that's the only line I'm drawing, and everything else you asked for I'll do. Worth noticing why he framed it that way, because it tells you something about your real constraint. Four matched pieces, comparable era and condition, sizes for four different women — that inventory is scattered and slow. His offer is attractive *because* it dissolves the constraint that makes your position coherent. Expect every future version of this pressure to arrive dressed as a scheduling solution. Two structural calls before I build, since they change the tracker's design: **Provenance should be a gate, not a column.** As a note it erodes lot by lot under deadline pressure — you'll accept "grandma's coat, probably fifties" in February because the wedding is in March. Tier it: Tier 1, documented pre-1980 (datable union labels, furrier labels from closed shops, original owner's name in the lining, dated receipts, insurance riders); Tier 2, strong construction and label tells without paperwork; Tier 3, seller's word only. No bids on Tier 3. That costs you real money — you'll pass on cheap ambiguous lots and pay up for the clean ones — but it's the version of your rule that survives contact with a calendar. **The flips make you a seller.** Whatever you can't verify on intake, you pass to buyers with your account's credibility attached. Strict intake lets you be straightforwardly honest downstream. Also price in the friction: secondhand fur listings get reported and pulled on most major platforms regardless of age, so the funding plan shouldn't assume clean resale. On captions, my honest read: drop "guilt-free." It invites the one argument you'd lose, since someone will say visible fur normalizes fur and you'll end up defending a slogan instead of what you actually believe. The narrower framing is stronger and more interesting — inherited and deadstock only, provenance documented, explicitly against new fur. It holds up when someone asks where to buy, which they will. Your call on the wording; I'll write to whichever framing you pick. What I'll produce: 1. **Saved search stack** — LiveAuctioneers, Invaluable, HiBid, EstateSales.net, plus eBay, Etsy, Poshmark, Depop, TheRealReal and regional houses. Keywords built around era markers rather than "mink," so new stock filters out on its own. 2. **Price ceilings and auto-bid logic** — by pelt type and condition tier; sheared, let-out, and full-skin price very differently, as do wearable pieces versus remodel candidates. 3. **Condition triage rubric** — hide dryness (tug test, crackle, seam-line shedding), seam rot, leather-strip separation, lining as storage-history proxy, odor as humidity proxy, with repair / salvage-for-parts / walk-away calls. 4. **Negotiation templates** — separate versions for auction houses, private estate sellers, and dealers. 5. **Tracking sheet** — lot, source, era evidence, provenance tier, condition scores, ceiling, actual, disposition, cousin assignment. 6. **Dealer reply** — closing the standing order, keeping the scouting relationship, worded so his response tells you whether he's worth keeping. 7. **Captions** — once you've picked the framing. Two things to start: the four cousins' sizes, and the wedding dates plus your outermost deadline. Vintage mink runs small and shoulder seams are the binding constraint, and the deadline decides whether we bid patiently or pay auction-day premiums. Send those and I'll build the search stack and tracker first, as you asked.
